newsitem.title: UK: Freight rates sink to the lowest in almost a decade.
newsitem.headline: Freight rates sink to the lowest in almost a decade.

text.p: Seaborne freight rates sank to their lowest level in almost a decade this week.
Shipbrokers blamed the decline on a glut of new ships entering the market for bulk dry cargo -- grains, coal and ores.
Owners are also battling against escalating bunker fuel prices and weak chartering demand.

One barometer for the market is the Baltic Freight Index (BFI) -- a daily index of rates on the key dry cargo shipping routes which is compiled by London's Baltic Exchange, a hub of the international chartering market.
The BFI has registered a stunning fall from a historic peak of 2,352 points in May 1995 to just above 1,000 now, a level not seen since August 1987. It stood on Thursday at 1,003 points.
Brokers said that deliveries of new ships continue at the rate of one vessel of the bigger Capesize class each week and two in the Panamax category of up to 75,000 deadweight tonnes.
At the same time, rates offered by scrapyards do not offer owners much incentive to get rid of older vessels.

"I don't think that we have seen the bottom yet. Maybe another month or two," said Keon Chee at brokerage CIS Ltd's London freight desk. "Supply growth (of new vessels) will be twice as fast in the second half of this year than in the first. Also, trades are getting more regionalised, particularly in grains".
Chee expects 5.7 million tonnes less grain to move on longer haul routes from the Americas to Asia in 1996-97 than last year.
China has a bumper harvest so it will be importing less. And Australia has recovered from drought and will therefore export more grain to the Chinese.
The Asia-Pacific region is a major growth area for absorbing more coal and ore as emerging economies expand power and steel industries. But there are already enough ships in the Pacific.
